method.two_granularities: PROP co-mention = both entities in the SAME chunk (mean 102.9 chars, i.e. one sentence) -- a strict test. DOC co-mention = both entities somewhere in the same source document. WASDE yield/stocks revisions are the primary information shock that re-prices the US balance sheet; downward yield/stocks surprises are bullish, upward bearish.

The white premium (refining margin = London #5 minus NY #11) is the defining driver of white sugar; when refining margins widen, the #5 price is pulled up relative to raws as refiners bid for spot refined supply.
A lower global soyoil/vegoil stocks-to-use ratio signals a tighter balance sheet and raises price; a higher ratio loosens it.
A lower global soybean/meal stocks-to-use ratio signals a tighter balance sheet that raises meal price; a higher ratio loosens it.
A narrow RSM discount to soymeal reduces RSM's substitution attractiveness while a wide soymeal premium pulls demand into RSM; the spread mechanically anchors RSM price to the protein complex.
Cheap feed wheat (Argentine/Mercosur) substitutes for corn in southern Brazilian livestock rations when the wheat-corn spread compresses, easing corn feed demand.

Soybeans and corn compete for the same Northeast China spring acreage; higher corn prices (or stronger corn subsidies) pull acres away from non-GMO soybeans, tightening domestic supply and raising DCE No.1 price.
Cheap feed wheat (incl. Argentine/imported) can substitute for corn in southern Brazil rations, lowering corn feed demand when the spread compresses.
Apparel/mill consumption tracks global consumer spending and retail inventories; strong demand draws down stocks and raises lint prices.

Retaliatory tariffs on US-origin cotton redirect Chinese demand to Brazil/Australia, widening origin differentials and pressuring ICE while supporting alternatives.
Drought during safrinha vegetative/flowering stages depletes soil moisture from a crop largely grown on residual rainfall, sharply reducing yield and lifting price.
US rice competes with corn for Mid-South acreage and water; relative returns shift planted area between them.
In food and feed use, wheat and rice are partial caloric substitutes; sharp wheat moves can spill into rice demand and policy responses.

Expanding Brazilian sorghum (sorgo) as a safrinha alternative and feed substitute eases corn demand and competes for the same second-crop acreage.
Feed barley substitutes for maize in EU and Black Sea rations when price-competitive, easing maize demand.
Brazil's large poultry and hog sectors (and exports thereof) consume most corn domestically; expanding herds raise interior demand and price, especially in deficit Northeast/South.

US Section 301/retaliatory tariffs redirect global corn trade flows and origin differentials, indirectly shifting EU import parity ambiguously.
